title: Written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34)
hookLine: I will write my law in their hearts

cards: A few things never need looking up. They're just in you. Your phone number from childhood.
The words to a song you haven't heard in twenty years. A grandmother's recipe you make without measuring. The Lord's Prayer, maybe, or a psalm.
You don't consult the paper. It comes up out of you, even at three in the morning. That's a very different kind of knowing from a rule posted on a wall.
Jeremiah, with Jerusalem's fall drawing near, heard God promise that kind of knowing.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah."
A covenant is a binding relationship, sealed with promises on both sides, more like a marriage than a contract.
The covenant at Sinai was written on stone tablets, and the people, Jeremiah says, broke it, though God had been like a husband to them. So what's new?
"I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." Same God. Same people.
Same law: the Hebrew word is torah, teaching.

teach.h: NOT ON STONE, ON THE HEART.
teach.b: But written in a new place: not on stone, on the heart.

teach.h: ALL SHALL KNOW ME, THE LEAST TOO.
teach.b: Then: "they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them." No one will need to teach a neighbor to know the Lord. And last: "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more."
Here readers differ, and it matters to say it carefully. Jewish readers hear a promise to Israel: the same covenant, renewed and finally taken to heart.
Christians hear it fulfilled in Jesus: at the Last Supper he speaks of the cup as the new covenant in his blood, and the letter to the Hebrews quotes this whole passage.
In the King James Bible, those words over the cup read: "This cup is the new testament in my blood."

teach.h: I WILL WRITE IT IN THEIR HEARTS.
teach.b: There, testament means covenant. This week: the servant, the thirsty, pe'er, a prophet too young, the potter, the city's peace, and now, the heart.

how: Christians hear the new covenant named at communion, in the words over the cup; some also memorize scripture, and Jeremiah 31:31–34 is read in Lent and at services focused on forgiveness.

the same torah, God's teaching, written in a new place: the heart.

Luke 22:20: this cup is the new testament in my blood. testament there means covenant.
Jewish and Christian readers hear this promise the same way
Jewish readers hear Israel's covenant renewed; Christians hear it fulfilled in Jesus.

games.q: the old covenant is broken, and the city is about to fall. what does God promise through Jeremiah?
o: a stricter law, carved deeper into stone.
his law written on their hearts.
an end to any covenant at all.
games.why: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts." not tougher stone. a different place to write.

practice: Choose something short to learn by heart, a verse, a line of a prayer, the psalm you picked to keep this year, or today's line, I will write it in their hearts, and say it slowly in your mind, then again without looking, then again more slowly.
Notice which words slip away and which stay; you're not memorizing for a test, just letting something move from the page into you. If you pray, you can pray the words as you learn them.
